repos.title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD) and Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD) for few-step distillation of multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs). The authors apply both to build NitroFusion2 from Z-Image-Turbo. TSAD attaches discriminator heads to intermediate text-token states, which depend on the image through joint attention. ACD conditions the frozen discriminator backbone on one of six image-grounded fields (typography, object, style, background, action, layout) or on the full caption, sampled per training step. At one step, NitroFusion2 scores 43.34 on LongText-EN and 47.78 on LongText-CN, versus 29.18 and 36.85 for TwinFlow. It scores 86.48 on DPG-Bench, above 84.86 for eight-step Z-Image-Turbo, and 75.86 on GenEval, versus 75.01. At two steps, Z-Image-Turbo++ scores higher on some metrics but uses 12B parameters, versus 6B here. Limitations: one-step output still struggles with complex scenes, sample diversity drops, ACD shows a seesaw effect across aspects, and layer selection is empirical.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Adversarial distillation has read only image features, and MMDiT text tokens offer an unused alternative.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work conditions discriminators on text but reads adversarial features only from the image.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: TSAD attaches heads to text-stream attention outputs, and ACD picks one aspect cue per training step.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: At one step, NitroFusion2 leads all five benchmarks and is on par with an eight-step reference on GenEval.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining limits are complex scenes at one step, reduced sample diversity, and a seesaw effect across cues.

digest_headlines.heading: AI use statement
digest_headlines.headline: The AI use statement says generative tools supported data, implementation, drafting and figures, not hypotheses or framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility statement
digest_headlines.headline: The reproducibility statement points to method sections, training setup, cue list, pseudo-code, and public release upon acceptance.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the training setup, cue categories, layer choices, per-dimension results, and open-weight comparisons.

repos.title: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder
repos.paper_summary:
CAPTOR is a training-free method that builds a term-by-patch compatibility matrix for a frozen image encoder from captions alone, with no text encoder and no gradient steps. It clusters patch tokens into visual words, describes each captioned image by the share of its patches in each word, and scores each term by how those shares differ between images whose captions mention it and those that do not. Each signature is divided by a permutation-null 95th percentile over 200 caption shuffles, so terms of different frequency share one scale. The matrix factors into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row.

On COCO, scored on cells one object owns, CAPTOR reaches 0.565 mIoU against 0.502 for the strongest training-free baseline. It is level with Talk2DINO, a text alignment trained on the same backbone, on COCO, Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline that reads a pathology text encoder by 0.160 mIoU. The stated limits include untested attributes, relations and negation, a hard partition that cannot separate patches sharing a word, and captions that supervise the table.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Counting caption words over frozen image patches can build a text-query matrix without any text encoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing grounding methods read a text encoder or train an alignment, while caption-counting predecessors share only the supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: CAPTOR factorizes the compatibility matrix into a term-by-word table and a per-image word map, with no gradient.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental setup
digest_headlines.headline: The table is counted from captions alone, and every reported number is measured once on a held-out reporting half.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: On COCO, CAPTOR reaches 0.565 mIoU, leading training-free baselines and level with trained Talk2DINO on mIoU.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: CAPTOR's vocabulary is limited to terms captions name often, and patches sharing a visual word cannot be separated.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Counting over captioned images can ground text in image encoders that have no text encoder.

digest_headlines.heading: CRediT authorship contribution statement
digest_headlines.headline: Elad Yoshai is credited with methodology and software, and Natan Shaked with supervision and project administration.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of competing interest
digest_headlines.headline: The authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could influence the work reported.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: All data are public and de-identified, and code to reproduce every number will be released upon acceptance.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process
digest_headlines.headline: The authors used Claude for text editing, checking reported numbers against records, and writing analysis code.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists abbreviations, dataset and protocol settings, COCO ablations, image rankings, timing and a SAM 3 comparison.

repos.title: RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking
repos.paper_summary: RAGCompass is a retriever router for retrieval-augmented generation. Given a query and the passage sets from five retrievers (dense, BM25, SPLADE-v3, ColBERTv2, HippoRAG2), it fine-tunes a Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B to score each passage set. Training uses KL divergence against a target distribution built from the answer F1 each set yields with a fixed Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reader. A two-layer transformer comparison head, with no retriever-specific parameters, reads all candidate representations jointly. On four QA datasets, test answer F1 is 0.3552, versus 0.2782 for the best fixed retriever and 0.3203 for static-weight mixing. The fine-tuned scorer alone reaches 0.3412, and the head adds 1.4pp. The oracle reaches 0.7508. Recall@5 rises 5.0 points. On held-out corpus, retriever, and reader splits, RAGCompass keeps most of its gain, while three query-only routers do not beat the best fixed retriever. Limitations: one reader plus one alternative reader, retrieval depth fixed at k=5, one reranker size, reimplemented baselines, and a 3.9% decision overhead measured on one device that excludes running all retrievers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Retriever choice varies by query, and an oracle picking per query reaches 0.75 F1 against 0.28 for the best fixed retriever.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior routers read queries or retriever identities rather than retrieved passages, and none was tested under a shift.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Routing is cast as reranking evidence sets, with a reranker trained to match the answer F1 each set yields.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Five retrievers are routed across four question-answering datasets, with generalization tested by holding out a dataset, a retriever, or the reader.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: RAGCompass reaches 0.3552 test F1, +7.7pp over the best fixed retriever and +3.5pp over the strongest baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Utility supervision beats relevance supervision by 2.11pp, while score coupling changes results by less than seed noise.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: RAGCompass outperforms every compared router at 3.9% of generation pipeline cost and keeps most of its gain under unseen conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results rest on one reader, one retrieval depth, one backbone scale, and reimplemented baselines, so transfer is untested beyond those.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers encoding and head ablations, retrieval metrics, majority vote, depth and data-size checks, baseline details, per-dataset results, and language-model router costs.

repos.title: GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats
repos.paper_summary: GaussianRenderFormer is a transformer that renders 3D Gaussian splats directly into images, with no rasterizer in the renderer. Each Gaussian is one token in a view-independent encoder initialized from RenderFormer's pretrained mesh-renderer weights. A view-dependent decoder turns 4×4-pixel patches of camera rays into pixels by cross-attending to those tokens, with 2D rotary embeddings of each Gaussian's projected center and a projected footprint added to the attention keys. Training uses 26,820 Objaverse splats, each pruned to 20,000 Gaussians, with an L1 loss in log encoding plus LPIPS. On 300 unseen objects, the model reaches 38.08 dB PSNR against renders of the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is 3.9 dB at camera distance 1.15 and 6.8 dB at 1.7. The model scores 38.02 dB on the development held-out set and only 0.17 dB higher on training objects, so the authors report the gap is not one of generalization. They attribute it to a decoder bottleneck but note that under-training is not ruled out. Limitations include lower quality and speed than rasterization, support only for single objects viewed from outside, no view-dependent color or relighting, and dependence on RenderFormer's pretrained weights.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: No learned renderer for 3D Gaussian splats existed, so this paper tests whether a transformer can output images directly.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work renders Gaussians only with hand-written rasterizers, while learned renderers cover meshes, points or implicit scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: The rasterizer that GaussianRenderFormer replaces projects, sorts and blends Gaussians, while RenderFormer renders meshes with two transformer stages.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each Gaussian becomes one token, and the view decoder gets projected centers, footprints and four-by-four-pixel patches.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses 26,820 Objaverse objects, each pruned to 20,000 Gaussians from splats of 50,000, with ground-truth renders.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 300 unseen objects the model scores 38.08 dB against the full splat, below the 44.02 dB of rasterizing the same pruned input.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The model is several dB below rasterizing, hundreds of times slower, and limited to single objects in one camera configuration.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A network renders a given Gaussian set without a rasterizer, but the gap to rasterizing remains and the result is not yet competitive.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists camera-path and real-capture results, supporting measurements, reproducibility settings, and licenses.

repos.title: Rewrite, Then Veto: Rewriter-Agnostic Edit Gating for LLM-Based Post-OCR Correction
repos.paper_summary: Rewrite, Then Veto proposes EditVeto, a gate placed after a full-context LLM rewrite of OCR transcripts that reverts edits the gate judges unhelpful. The rewrite is character-aligned to the OCR input, split into edit blocks, and each block is kept or reverted by a 0.6B-parameter Qwen3 gate. Oracle analysis motivates the design: given true error locations, per-span generation with Qwen3-8B scores worse than no correction (cMER 0.0562 vs. 0.0275 on development), while vetoing a full rewrite's edits helps. The gate is trained on rewrites from two Qwen3 models and frozen. On the eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, it improves all five rewriters tested, including two unseen in training: weighted cMER falls by 0.0026 to 0.0044 and the preference score rises by 0.15 to 0.25 (paired bootstrap, p≈0.0002). On published competition outputs, it lowers cMER for three of four teams but raises it for the winning run (0.0050 to 0.0065). A second, disclosed look with LoRA-tuned rewriters and an edit-pool ensemble reaches cMER 0.0069, mostly from fine-tuning and pooling rather than the gate. Limitations: a single global threshold, one seed per configuration, and results on one benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: LLM rewrites of OCR transcripts also change correct text, so the paper proposes a learned gate that vetoes collateral edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier post-OCR methods generate corrections directly, whereas this work filters a finished LLM rewrite at the level of edit blocks.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Definition
digest_headlines.headline: The task is scored by normalized cMER and a preference score, and a veto keeps a subset of rewrite edits with a bounded error.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A full-context rewrite is split into character edit blocks, and a 0.6B-parameter gate keeps or reverts each block.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation uses eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, the official scorer, paired bootstrap tests, and three separately reported test looks.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation: Oracle Analysis (Development Set)
digest_headlines.headline: With oracle error spans, per-span generation is worse than no correction, while vetoing edits of a full rewrite lowers cMER from 0.0247 to 0.0229.

digest_headlines.heading: Learned Gate: Development Results
digest_headlines.headline: On development data, the frozen gate lowers weighted cMER for all five rewriters, including two never seen in training.

digest_headlines.heading: Test Results
digest_headlines.headline: On test, the frozen gate lowers cMER for all five rewriters by 0.0026–0.0044, but raises it for the winning competition run.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The gate helps the tested rewriters, and a pooled fine-tuned ensemble reaches 0.0069 cMER, behind the winner's 0.0050.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix holds the Proposition 1 proof and checks, development and test tables, third-look design, and compute usage.

repos.title: TSFM Meets LLM: Context as Covariates
repos.paper_summary: CoCo (Context as Covariates) is a forecasting framework in which an LLM turns textual context into forecast and confidence covariates that guide a Chronos2 time series foundation model (TSFM). The paper also builds a pipeline that annotates real time series with LLM-generated text to create multimodal training data. The LLM, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, is first fine-tuned with GRPO, using a reward tied to the forecast improvement its covariates produce. The forecast covariate is the LLM's median forecast. The confidence covariate is the per-step variance across LLM rollouts, normalized by history variance. Chronos2 is then fine-tuned on covariates from the aligned LLM. Synthetic annotations come from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Evaluation covers 30 datasets and 95 settings in finance, weather, macroeconomics, traffic, and security, with up to 12% MAE improvement over TSFM and LLM baselines, including GPT-4o, and up to 70% improvement over GPT-4o on traffic. A theorem bounds the gap between the real-text risk of a model trained on synthetic text and the best achievable real-text risk by 2L(εr+εs), under Lipschitz and embedding-approximation assumptions. Stated limitations: fine-tuning is sequential, and the method does not yet assess whether text is misleading.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Textual context carries forecasting signals that numerical foundation models cannot use, motivating a paired LLM and TSFM design.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior text-aided forecasters are domain-specific, LLM-centric, or ignore TSFMs, so this work targets a zero-shot, domain-agnostic setup.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Multimodal forecasting is defined as mapping numerical history and per-timestamp text annotations to a future forecast.

digest_headlines.heading: Synthetic Multimodal Dataset Generation
digest_headlines.headline: An LLM generates annotations from numerical windows that resemble real text in forecast-trend similarity, supporting sim-to-real transfer.

digest_headlines.heading: Context as Covariates
digest_headlines.headline: CoCo feeds LLM forecast and confidence covariates to a TSFM, with the LLM tuned by GRPO and the TSFM tuned afterward.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CoCo with Qwen3-4B and Chronos2 has the best mean MAE, 0.719, across 30 datasets and 95 settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work proposes a text reliability check and joint fine-tuning, because CoCo degrades when text is misleading.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The acknowledgments name partial National Science Foundation support under Grant No. 2148186.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, theorem proofs, probe and ablation tables, latency, prompts and societal impact.

repos.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
repos.paper_summary: This perspective paper proposes AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person, as the second half of AI's endgame beside artificial general intelligence. It names the system that would realize it a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, proactive companion. Its conceptual core is the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory. The design space is organized as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and trust. The paper defines six properties a symbiont must have and reviews five technology lines (foundation models, agents, memory, world models, wearables) by what each provides and lacks. It also covers risks, governance, and an evaluation agenda with ten dimensions and twenty-three open problems. The excerpt reports no experiments or measured results, so its evaluation content is a research agenda.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: AI progress is scored by what machines do alone, leaving everyday losses of memory and support unaddressed.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Where We Stand
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work on human–AI roles and augmentation has not targeted augmenting one particular person across a life.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Technical Foundations
digest_headlines.headline: Five existing technology lines supply most parts a symbiont needs, but none targets augmenting one particular person.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Conceptual Foundations
digest_headlines.headline: The paper defines a cognitive gap, six required properties, and a symbiosis loop that organizes its design space.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Sensing and Interacting
digest_headlines.headline: A symbiont must borrow its senses and voice from wearable devices, favoring private input and private output.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Personal Context and Lifelong Knowledge
digest_headlines.headline: Context, working state, and knowledge form one record across three timescales, fed by one entry point for all sources.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Understanding a Person
digest_headlines.headline: The personal model fuses observation with self-report across seven layers, on any backbone, and declares its own limits.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 Living Alongside
digest_headlines.headline: A fast loop and a slow loop let the symbiont speak privately at the right moment, with silence as a formal choice.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 The Ladder of Assistance
digest_headlines.headline: Assistance is organized in three tiers, from completing tasks to thinking with the person to living among others.

digest_headlines.heading: 10 Growing Together
digest_headlines.headline: The symbiont and the person change together, and each model update must account for the system's own actions.

digest_headlines.heading: 11 The Personal Runtime
digest_headlines.headline: A personal runtime spanning devices and applications is needed, since no single application can hold continuity.

digest_headlines.heading: 12 Trust
digest_headlines.headline: Trust is treated as architecture: authorization climbs in steps, and the system must be useful at low authorization.

digest_headlines.heading: 13 Whom It Serves
digest_headlines.headline: Knowledge workers come first to verify the approach, while children, acute crisis cases, and compelled settings should wait.

digest_headlines.heading: 14 A World of Augmented Individuals
digest_headlines.headline: In a speculative street scene, every person is augmented, and augmented people and embodied robots share one cognitive core.

digest_headlines.heading: 15 The Risks of Augmentation
digest_headlines.headline: Augmentation creates risks beyond the system: attribution, invisibility, reach into others' lives, and pressure to adopt.

digest_headlines.heading: 16 Governing Augmentation
digest_headlines.headline: Symbionts would follow declared assistance policies, though proving abstention remains an open problem alongside norms and law.

digest_headlines.heading: 17 Evaluation and Research Agenda
digest_headlines.headline: Success is measured by the person's unaided gain, not the AI's output, across ten dimensions and four study designs.

digest_headlines.heading: 18 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A lifelong personal companion should be judged by what the person can do, and three regions of the map remain blank.

repos.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
repos.paper_summary: PolicyIK is a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that learns high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms through a joint-position interface. The policy accumulates its actions into a joint reference, observes that reference relative to the measured joints, and uses two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain. Its reward combines tracking, a running-best progress term, and a dwell term so the policy both reaches and holds a tolerance of 1 mm and 0.2°. In simulation on a 7-DoF arm, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps mean errors over the final second within tolerance on 93.5% of held-out tasks, rising to 98.9% with a deployment protocol. Ablations show each design choice lowers single-attempt success by 1.8 to 9.2 points when removed. On two physical arms, trained with FlashSAC, PolicyIK reaches and holds more tasks than four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, it executes the end-effector commands of the π0.5 VLA policy with 95.7% success across ten adapted LIBERO-Object tasks. Limitations: the policy's real-arm and pick-and-place results are reported with fewer detailed numbers in the text provided, and inference takes 0.035 ms on CPU against a 33 ms control period.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Policies that output end-effector poses inherit inverse kinematics accuracy, and precise inverse kinematics is hard to build.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior learned reaching controllers reach millimeter to centimeter accuracy, and sub-millimeter results need a classical solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Success is defined as mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2°, posed as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method accumulates actions into a joint reference, scales them by error, and rewards each new best error and every step within tolerance.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: In simulation, one attempt reaches 93.5% strict success, rising to 98.9% with the deployment protocol.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Hardware training with the same terminal-phase design reaches and holds more tasks than all four classical controllers.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists simulation setup, reward and training settings, deployment protocol, baseline tuning, hardware controller settings, and xArm7 results.

repos.title: $Φ$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction
repos.paper_summary: ΦasmaNet is a compact neural surrogate that maps the 11 input features of a precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signal (IMRPhenomXPHM) to its phase-averaged optimal SNR in one detector (LIGO-Hanford) at a fixed Advanced LIGO design PSD. Learned input tokens pass through an ordered cascade of attention-based Φ-Stages, each with a subspace-mixing Φ-Refractor module, followed by gated top-down Φ-Feedback iterations. Labels come from PyCBC, with training sets from 10^5 to 10^6 samples. At 10^6 samples, the model reaches 100−MAPE = 98.73% on the held-out test set, 99.29% after monotonic PCHIP calibration, and 99.39% with R² = 0.9998 for ρ > 8. Under a matched protocol, it outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet, and Transformer-encoder baselines at every scale, using about 732k parameters. On one GPU it sustains about 1.2×10^5 SNR evaluations per second, processing 10^6 injections in about 8.3 s, roughly two orders of magnitude faster than waveform-and-inner-product computation on a 16-core CPU. Limitations: one detector, one PSD, and ρ < 200. Predictions do not transfer to other PSDs or detector networks, and the paper does not include full ablations attributing gains to individual components.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Selection-effect studies need SNRs for millions of injections, and a neural surrogate could replace the per-source calculation.

digest_headlines.heading: The Challenge of Signal-to-Noise Ratio Calculation
digest_headlines.headline: Direct SNR evaluation is costly per source, and the cost recurs at every likelihood step of a hierarchical analysis.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior SNR surrogates use plain multilayer perceptrons on low-dimensional inputs, and the closest package reduces spins to one effective spin.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Labels are phase-averaged single-detector SNRs at 1000 Mpc, with 11 input features and a log10 regression target.

digest_headlines.heading: Classic Deep Learning Architectures
digest_headlines.headline: Three baselines serve for comparison: a four-hidden-layer MLP, a 1D ResNet with 2 blocks per stage, and a Transformer encoder with four layers.

digest_headlines.heading: $\Phi$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Network with Recursive Feedback
digest_headlines.headline: ΦasmaNet refines eight learned tokens through three Φ-Stages and two Φ-Feedback passes, each stage adding a subspace-mixing module.

digest_headlines.heading: Architectural Novelty and Design Rationale
digest_headlines.headline: Authors frame the contribution as staged inductive bias composition, with stage ordering treated as motivation rather than a verified property.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Protocol, Hyperparameters, and Evaluation Metrics
digest_headlines.headline: Every model shares one protocol tuned on the MLP baseline, so the ΦasmaNet comparison uses settings not chosen for it.

digest_headlines.heading: Architectures Comparison Across Dataset Sizes
digest_headlines.headline: ΦasmaNet has the highest post-calibration accuracy at every size, reaching 99.29 at 1M samples versus 98.06 for ResNet.

digest_headlines.heading: Best-model Diagnostics
digest_headlines.headline: On the SNR above 8 subset, calibrated accuracy is 99.39, and inference runs at about 1.2×10^5 evaluations per second.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors support ΦasmaNet for simulation-driven selection-effect studies and list its single-detector, fixed-PSD limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Code Availability
digest_headlines.headline: Training code for ΦasmaNet and its three baselines is publicly released on GitHub.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists out-of-the-box results on YearPredictionMSD, Covertype and Epsilon, with no dataset-specific tuning.

repos.title: You don't need long context
repos.paper_summary: This paper argues that frontier language models do not need long contexts for long-horizon or long-input tasks. It tests three context-management methods: end-of-conversation compaction (EoCC), which replaces history with a bounded state summary when the context crosses a threshold; selective input reading, which stores long inputs as files the agent reads with Bash tools; and single-action compaction (SAC), which runs one action per fresh context from a compact semantic state. Evaluation covers six long-horizon benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks) and FRAMES (824 questions), and seven long-input benchmarks, including LongBench v2 (503 questions) and BABILong (550 questions). Principal accuracy runs use Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol. The authors report that EoCC usually matches or slightly improves full-history accuracy on long-horizon tasks, with modest losses elsewhere. Cloud throughput measurements on H100 nodes show 3.6x to 7x more decoded tokens per second at a 16K context window than at 256K. The authors state that the evidence does not rule out tasks where long context helps.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Serving at 256K tokens costs 3.6x to 7x more per generated token than serving at 16K for open-weight models.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Three context regimes are compared on six long-horizon and seven long-input benchmarks with frontier and open-weight models.

digest_headlines.heading: Long-horizon tasks don’t need long contexts
digest_headlines.headline: Compacting context keeps long-horizon accuracy between -3.7 and +5.6 percentage points of baseline for Claude Opus 4.5.

digest_headlines.heading: Long-input tasks don’t need long contexts
digest_headlines.headline: Selective reading of input files with compaction as fallback matches or beats full-input baselines on almost all long-input benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Compaction can be performed after every action
digest_headlines.headline: Single-action compaction preserves or improves Claude Opus 4.5 accuracy, while GPT 5.6 Sol drops 2.0 and 3.3 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
